title: Iris and the Yummy Pattern
markdown:
It was a day so bright the sky was practically giggling blue. Fluffy clouds danced, pushed by a whispering breeze that tried to tell the apple tree a secret and then forgot. In Teacher June’s garden everything was happy-happy: bees already at work, a ladybug on a leaf that Iris spotted from way over there, a mat all colours of the rainbow. Momo the monkey swung from the big old apple tree — whoosh one way, whoosh the other, giggles like tinkly bells, ting-a-ling. June sat on the mat, sunny smile. Beside her, Iris the pattern-finder. Her brain was a busy buzzing hive, always looking for how things fit together.

“Momo, so much fun!” June’s voice was warm as a hug. “Iris, this flower — a cheerful splash of sunshine.” Petals like yellow ribbons, a fuzzy middle like a tiny wobbly hat.

Then June’s smile wobbled. The picnic basket looked sad and empty. “Our fruit snacks are almost gone. A few blueberries. One lonely strawberry.”

Iris’s ears perked. “Running out? We need more yummy things. What if we run out before snack time?”

Momo stopped mid-whoosh, landed with a soft thump. Tail wiggle. “More yummy things? Yes please!” He adored juicy fruit. But where? The garden was huge. Tastiest treats played hide-and-seek. They had peeked under leafy bushes that tickled toes and behind giggling sunflowers. No extras.

Zoom. A stripey buzzy bee with fuzzy legs hummed past their noses. Bzzzzzzzzzz. It zipped with purpose toward a bright flower not far away: big velvet petals, tall proud stem, something interesting in the middle.

Iris’s pattern-finding eyes followed. The bee landed on the fuzzy, slightly darker middle. Bzzz. Legs wiggling. Zip — another flower. Landed: the middle again. Not random. Always the middle.

“Look!” She tugged June’s sleeve. “The bee always goes to the middle! A super-duper pattern!”

June’s eyes twinkled. “A brilliant find.” She pointed. “Lovely colourful petals like little flags. A strong stem reaching for the sun. And right in the middle — the sweet nectar. Yummy juice the bees love.”

Iris nodded, brain whirring. Petals. Stem. Middle. Bee to the middle. Pattern. Could it help them find more yummy things? A happy flutter.

“If the bee likes the middle, and we find flowers that look like this, maybe yummy things grow nearby!”

Momo bounced. “Flowers like this? Pretty petals and a busy middle?”

“Let’s follow the bee’s trail. Eyes peeled for that shape. Iris, you lead.”

Off they went, picnic basket empty enough to need filling. Momo scampered ahead, tail helping him leap tiny roots. Leap, scramble, a near-tumble into a puddle that was not berry-shaped. Iris walked head-tilted, scanning left and right for that flower shape, counting middles under her breath. One flower had petals but a closed middle; she skipped it. Another was all stem and showing off. Then more special flowers, petals seeming to shout come this way. Each time they found one, they looked around, excitement growing, June keeping the empty strawberry company so it would not feel left behind.

They almost followed a bee that went to a thistle, which had a middle but the wrong kind of welcome. Iris shook her head. Pattern, but not this pattern. Just past a patch of bright red flowers with wide-open middles — just like the first, velvet flags, busy centres — a whole bush bursting with ripe juicy berries. Plump, red, glistening, hiding behind the last sunflower they had already checked this morning when they were looking in the wrong places. Momo squealed like a tiny trumpet. Toot-toot. He loved berries. June laughed, which sounded like another kind of bell.

“Yippee! So many!” He plucked one, cheeks puffing. Munch, munch.

June clapped softly. “You found them by the flower pattern. Snack time is saved.”

Iris beamed. “The bee likes the middle. We found flowers like that — pretty petals, special middle — and then berries. The pattern told us where to look.”

June knelt, a warm hug, and left the my-clever off. Petals a welcome sign. Stem to stand tall. The middle helping the flower, and the bees, work as a team. She did not send them hunting dens and puddles.

Momo, mouth still full, juice on his chin, nodded. “Flower parts help bees, bees help flowers, flowers make berries. Yum.”

Iris looked at the bush, the flowers, a still-buzzing bee. “A yummy pattern that helps everyone.” She put the lonely strawberry back in the basket beside the new berries, so it would not be lonely anymore, and did not announce that the world was a grand adventure. Momo swung once more, then came down for seconds.
